en: 1.1.1 Discrete and Continuous Quantities Discrete Quantities: Separate, countable items with specific values. They can be counted one by one. Number of students in a classroom Number of cars in a parking lot Continuous Quantities: Can take any value within a range. They flow smoothly without breaks. Temperature of water Speed of a moving car :)Continuous( 💡 Analogy: Stairs vs Ramp Stairs represent discrete data (fixed steps). A ramp represents continuous data (any point). Discrete (Stairs) Continuous (Ramp)

en: 1.1.2 Introduction to Digital Systems A digital system is an electronic system that uses only two values: 0 and 1. These two values are called binary digits or bits. 0 represents OFF, LOW, or FALSE. 1 represents ON, HIGH, or TRUE. Why Use Digital Systems? / Advantage English Detail Urdu Translation ( ) Reliable Less affected by noise and interference. Accurate No loss of quality when copying data. Easy to Design Only two states (0 and 1) to handle. Programmable Can be easily controlled by software. Examples of Digital Systems Computers: Processes data as 0s and 1s. Smartphones: Stores photos and music as binary data. Digital Cameras: Captures images as binary code.

en: 1.1.3 Analog and Digital Signals ★ GOLDEN TOPIC Analog Signals Continuous signals that change smoothly over time, like a sine wave. (e.g., Human voice, traditional thermometers). Digital Signals Have only two levels: HIGH (1) and LOW (0). They jump instantly between values, creating a square wave. (e.g., Computer data). Analog Signal (Sine Wave) Digital Signal (Square Wave) HIGH(1) LOW(0) Feature Analog Data Digital Data Nature Continuous flow. Discrete, separate values (Bits). Reliability Low (affected by noise). High (resistant to noise).

en: 1.1.4 Boolean Algebra Boolean algebra (developed by George Boole) deals with only two values: TRUE (1) and FALSE (0). It is the foundation of digital electronics and computer programming. Concept Description Example Variables Letters that hold values 0 or 1. A, B, C, X, Y Operations Actions performed on variables. AND, OR, NOT Expressions Combinations of variables & operations. A AND B, Y = A + B 1.1.5 Boolean Operations 1. AND Operation ( · ) The AND operation gives output 1 ONLY when ALL inputs are 1. Expression: Y = A · B 💡 Real-life Example / A door with two locks. The door opens only when BOTH locks are unlocked.

en: Boolean Operations (Continued) 2. OR Operation ( + ) The OR operation gives output 1 when ANY input is 1. Expression: Y = A + B 💡 Real-life Example / A room with two doors. You can enter if EITHER door is open. 3. NOT Operation ( ' or ¯ ) The NOT operation inverts the input. It is a unary operation (operates on only one operand). If input is 1, output is 0. Expression: Y = A' or Y = A̅ 💡 Real-life Example / A room light switch. When switch is ON, room is lit. When OFF, room is dark.

en: 1.1.6 Truth Tables A truth table shows all possible input combinations and their corresponding outputs for a logic gate or circuit. How to create a truth table: 1. Count the number of inputs (n). 2. Calculate total rows = 2ⁿ. 3. List all input combinations in binary order. 4. Calculate output for each combination. 2-Input Example (n=2, Rows=4) Combinations Row 1 Row 2 Row 3 Row 4 3-Input Example (n=3, Rows=8)
